sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content:
Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language. In Class 12, we revise Key concepts  learned in Class 11 and explore advanced features.

Python programs are saved with the .py extension and executed by the Python interpreter line by line.

sections.heading: Data Types
sections.content:
Python has several built-in data types:

• int — whole numbers like 42, -7
• float — decimal numbers like 3.14, -0.5
• str — text like 'Hello', "World"
• bool — True or False
• list — ordered mutable sequence [1, 2, 3]
• tuple — ordered immutable sequence (1, 2, 3)
• dict — key-value pairs {'name': 'Asha', 'age': 17}
• set — unordered unique items {1, 2, 3}

codeBlocks.code:
x = 42          # int
y = 3.14        # float
name = 'Sumit'  # str
flag = True     # bool

print(type(x))  # <class 'int'>
print(type(y))  # <class 'float'>
codeBlocks.explanation: Use type() to check the data type of any variable.

sections.heading: Operators
sections.content:
Python supports the following categories of operators:

• Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, //, %, **
• Comparison: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=
• Logical: and, or, not
• Assignment: =, +=, -=, *=, /=
• Membership: in, not in
• Identity: is, is not

codeBlocks.code:
# Arithmetic
print(10 // 3)   # 3 (floor division)
print(10 % 3)    # 1 (modulus)
print(2 ** 8)    # 256 (exponentiation)

# Membership
fruits = ['apple', 'mango', 'banana']
print('mango' in fruits)     # True
print('orange' not in fruits)  # True
codeBlocks.explanation: Floor division (//) discards the decimal part. Modulus (%) returns the remainder.

sections.heading: Strings
sections.content:
Strings in Python are immutable sequences of characters. Common string methods include:

• upper(), lower(), title()
• strip(), lstrip(), rstrip()
• split(), join()
• replace(), find(), count()
• startswith(), endswith()
• len() — returns the length

codeBlocks.code:
s = '  Hello World  '
print(s.strip())          # 'Hello World'
print(s.strip().lower())  # 'hello world'

words = 'one,two,three'.split(',')
print(words)  # ['one', 'two', 'three']
print('-'.join(words))  # 'one-two-three'
codeBlocks.explanation: strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace. split() splits a string into a list.

sections.heading: Lists vs Tuples
sections.content:
Lists and Tuples are both sequences, but Lists are mutable (can be changed) while Tuples are immutable (cannot be changed after creation).

Use tuples when data should not change (e.g., coordinates, RGB values).
Use lists when you need to add, remove, or modify elements.

codeBlocks.code:
# List - mutable
marks = [85, 90, 78]
marks.append(95)
marks[0] = 88
print(marks)  # [88, 90, 78, 95]

# Tuple - immutable
coords = (28.6, 77.2)  # latitude, longitude
# coords[0] = 30  # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
codeBlocks.explanation: Attempting to modify a tuple raises a TypeError. This immutability makes tuples faster and safer for fixed data.
